_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: To Bei Bli’ei: waters in the ocean that swallow all the waters of the world that fall into it, carry them down to the deep and spit them out. This is what is written: “And the sea is not full” (Ecclesiastes 1:7).
rashi:a1.2: Me’anei: afflicted and downcast, because they were not in their own land.
rashi:a1.3: Ikshu: they grew bold and spoke harshly to the king. When they smelled the scent of their land, they thought they were near their land.
rashi:a2.1: Betigda: in a utensil. Another version: betinara, a barrel.
rashi:a2.2: Until their shoulders became disjointed: their shoulders slipped out of place.
rashi:a2.3: And they wore away and went: they wasted away and went to destruction.
rashi:a3.1: Mishna. He gives one lamb to the priest: as redemption, since either way one of them is a firstborn that opened the womb.
rashi:a3.2: A male and a female: and it is not known whether the male came out first, in which case it is a firstborn, or the female came out first, and there is no firstborn here.
rashi:a3.3: He designates a lamb: because of the uncertainty, and thereby removes from it [the donkey] the sanctity of a firstborn donkey.
rashi:a3.4: And it is for himself: he himself eats the lamb and does not give it to the priest, since the priest would be extracting from his fellow, and the burden is on him to bring witnesses that the male came out first. And there is no prohibition involved, since even with a definite firstborn donkey redeemed with a lamb there is sanctity neither in it nor in its redemption, as the mishna teaches: “And if it dies, one may derive benefit from it.” There is only [a question of] theft if he does not give the lamb to the priest, since it is a monetary matter; and here there is no theft, since it is uncertain.
rashi:a4.1: Two donkeys … a male and a female, he gives a lamb to the priest: for the male.
rashi:a4.2: Or two males and a female: one bore a male, and the other bore a male and a female.
rashi:a4.3: He gives one lamb to the priest: since there is one male that is certainly a firstborn. For the other, which is uncertain, since perhaps the female came out first, he designates a lamb and it is his own.
rashi:a4.4: Two males and two females: these are uncertain, since perhaps each one bore a male and a female, and perhaps the females came out first. Therefore the priest has nothing here; rather, he designates two lambs for them to abrogate their forbidden status, and they are his own.
rashi:a5.1: One had given birth etc., a male and a female, he designates a lamb and it is his own: since perhaps the one that had not given birth bore the female.
rashi:a6.1: As it is stated: “And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb”: this refers back to the first clause. That is to say: from where do we derive that a firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb? As it is stated: “And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.”
rashi:a6.2: Male or female: whether the lamb is male or female.
rashi:a6.3: And he may redeem with it many times: if the priest gave it back to the Israelite, and he has [other] firstborn donkeys, he can redeem them with it.
rashi:a6.4: It enters etc.: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a7.1: Gemara. Who taught it: [the ruling about] a donkey that had not given birth and bore two males, that he gives the priest only one lamb.
rashi:a7.2: Not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: as we say below, in the chapter HaLokeaḥ Ubar Parato (Bekhorot 17a): a ewe that had not given birth and bore two males, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says both go to the priest, since it is possible for the births to coincide exactly, so that both came out as one and both are firstborns.
rashi:a8.1: It is different there, as it is written: with a ewe.
rashi:a8.2: The males shall be the Lord’s: which implies two. But with a firstborn donkey, where “the males” is not written, even if it is possible for the births to coincide exactly, they are not consecrated.
rashi:a9.1: But let him derive from it: the firstborn of a non-kosher animal from a kosher animal.
rashi:a9.2: But the Merciful One restricted: “the males”; the extra letter heh [“the”] implies this one and not another.
rashi:a11.1: Granted, according to Rabbi Yirmeya, who does not establish it in accordance with Rabbi Yosei: since he explains the reason of the mishna as being that it is impossible for the births to coincide exactly, so that the head of one did not come out first and open the womb. That is why the mishna does not teach “their two heads came out as one,” as it teaches below (Bekhorot 17a) in connection with the statement of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: since it is not possible.
rashi:a11.2: But according to Abaye: [who holds] it is possible for the births to coincide exactly, and the reason [only one lamb is given] is the restriction of “the males,” let it teach “and their heads came out as one,” and we would learn a novelty from it.
rashi:a12.1: And furthermore, it is taught: explicitly, that even with a non-kosher animal Rabbi Yosei says both go to the priest.
rashi:a13.2: Rather, because it is stated “the males”: with the firstborn of a kosher animal, from which we learn that it is possible for births to coincide exactly, he said the same holds for a firstborn donkey.
tosafot:a1.1: Bei Bli’ei: Rashi explained: the waters of the ocean, which swallow all the waters of the world and spit them out by way of the deep, as it is written: “And the sea is not full.” But this is difficult, since just afterward it says that he poured it into a tigra, which is the name of a utensil; how, then, would they go down into the deep? If one explains [tigra as] a pit or a trench, it works out. And it may be that Bei Bli’ei is the name of a place, since it is said there [elsewhere]: “In Bei Bli’ei there are three statues: one with its hand on its head, one on its heart, and the last of them points with its hand behind it.”
tosafot:a3.1: A male and a female, he designates a lamb for himself: And if you say: according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who says it is possible for births to coincide exactly, if both came out at once the male is not consecrated, according to what was explained above, that the female interposes. Furthermore, we learn below in the second chapter (Bekhorot 17b): “A male and a female, the priest has nothing,” which seems to refer to “their two heads came out as one” in the first clause: the female cancels the male’s firstborn status, since she too opened the womb. If so, join the slight chance of their coming out at once to the even chance that the female came first, and the male’s coming first is the lesser chance. [Why, then, designate a lamb?] One may answer, as [the Gemara] argued above: in the case of a slight uncertainty they were stringent, [requiring him] to designate a lamb for himself.
tosafot:a4.1: His two donkeys had not given birth and they bore two males, he gives two lambs to the priest: Here it works out, since this was needed to teach us that one does not redeem [with one lamb] and then redeem again [with the same lamb] so long as it has not been given into the priest’s hand, as was argued above in this chapter (Bekhorot 4b). But below, in the second chapter, where the same case is taught with firstborns of kosher animals, one cannot say this. One may answer: it teaches us that we do not suppose, so as to leave the money with its owner, that one of them miscarried a shapeless mass whose fetus dissolved and the other bore two males. However, below, in the chapter Yesh Bekhor (Bekhorot 48b), the same case is taught with women, and one cannot say this, since each woman knows for herself what she bore. One may answer: since it taught it here, it taught it there. Alternatively, it prefers to spell out every case even where they are not needed, as it teaches “a male and a female, he gives one to the priest,” which is not needed at all.
tosafot:a4.2: Two males and a female, he gives one lamb to the priest: Apparently he also designates one lamb for himself because of the uncertainty. So it is evident below in the second chapter (Bekhorot 18b), where for two males and a female, one is his and one is the priest’s, because the sanctity of a firstborn takes effect on both of them. And so Rashi explained: he designates another lamb and it is his own.
tosafot:a7.1: Who taught it? Rabbi Yirmeya says: Not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: Rashi explained: who taught that [if a donkey] bore two males, he gives only one lamb to the priest? But this is difficult for his explanation, since here even Rabbi Yosei HaGelili agrees, as the mishna does not teach “and their two heads came out as one,” as it does in the second chapter (Bekhorot 17a); and since we did not see that they came out at once, we do not say out of uncertainty that they came out at once, even according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, since it is uncommon. One must explain: granted that in a case of uncertainty Rabbi Yosei HaGelili agrees that he gives the priest only one lamb, nevertheless, with a slight uncertainty it is good to be stringent and to designate a second lamb for himself.
gershom:a1.1: When he reached Bei Bli’ei: a place in the sea that swallows other waters. And some say this is the well of Miriam.
gershom:a2.1: That they were me’anei: like one exiled from his place, and they had no answer on their tongue.
gershom:a3.1: They spoke harshly before the king: when they sensed their soil, their hearts grew proud over their soil, and they spoke harshly before the king, answering him arrogantly.
gershom:a4.1: He said: to Rabbi Yehoshua: Do with them whatever you wish.
gershom:a5.1: He poured it into a tigra: into a utensil, a large jug.
gershom:a6.1: Until their shoulders slipped: out of place, and they wasted away and went.
gershom:a7.1: His donkey that had not given birth: that had never given birth until now, and it bore two males.
gershom:a8.1: He gives one lamb to the priest: as redemption for the one that came out first.
gershom:a9.1: And if it bore a male and a female and he does not know which came out first, [and perhaps it was] the male, which is sacred with firstborn sanctity, he designates one lamb to abrogate the sanctity of the uncertain firstborn, to abrogate its forbidden status.
gershom:a10.1: And it: that lamb belongs to the Israelite himself, is fully non-sacred, and may be eaten. What is the reason? Because we say: the burden of proof rests on the one who extracts from his fellow; and since the priest cannot bring proof that the male came out first, it belongs to the Israelite himself.
gershom:a11.1: A male and a female: one bore a male and one bore a female; he gives one lamb to the priest, for the one that bore the male.
gershom:a12.1: Two males and two females: each one bore a male and a female, and he does not know which came out first.
gershom:a13.1: The priest has nothing here: but he designates two lambs for himself.
gershom:a14.1: One had already given birth and one had never given birth until now, and they bore two males etc.
gershom:a15.1: As it is stated: “And the firstborn of a donkey…”: this “as it is stated” does not refer to the matter just said; it is a clause of its own. That is, what is written, “And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a seh,” does not mean only with a sheep: even with a goat, a male or a female, a large or a small one, an unblemished or a blemished one, it is fit to redeem with.
gershom:a16.1: And he may redeem with it many times: that is, if the lamb he gave the priest to redeem one firstborn donkey came back into his hand, because the priest sold it to him or gave it to him, he can redeem another firstborn donkey with that same lamb; whenever it comes into his hand he can redeem with it again. Or, if he designated it for himself as we said, and another firstborn donkey was born to him, he can certainly redeem it with that same lamb. And the lamb he designated for himself is fully non-sacred and enters the pen to be tithed with the rest of his sheep.
gershom:a17.1: And if it dies, one may derive benefit from it: an Israelite who designated a lamb to give to the priest for a definite firstborn donkey, and it died before he managed to give it to the priest: the priest may benefit from its hide and its carcass, since from the moment he designated it the priest acquired it, and it stands in his possession.
gershom:a18.1: As if it is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: he says in the other chapter that it is possible for births to coincide exactly, as we say: “Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says both go to the priest, as it is stated: ‘The males shall be the Lord’s.’” Here too, if it is Rabbi Yosei, he should have to give two lambs to the priest, since he holds it is possible for births to coincide exactly, so that both came out as one.
gershom:a19.1: It is different there: with a firstborn kosher animal, “the males shall be the Lord’s” implies both of them; but here, with the redemption of a firstborn donkey, “the males” is not written.
gershom:a20.1: But the Merciful One restricted “the males”: since it is written “the males,” which is superfluous after “all that opens the womb,” “the males” excludes the others: for these, which have inherent sanctity, “the males shall be the Lord’s,” both of them; but not with sanctity of value.
gershom:a21.1: Granted, according to Rabbi Yirmeya: who states flatly that it is not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei, that is why it does not teach here, with a donkey that had not given birth, “and their heads came out as one,” as it teaches in the mishna of the other chapter, where Rabbi Yosei takes part. Evidently this mishna is not Rabbi Yosei’s.
gershom:a22.1: But according to Abaye: who wants to establish it in accordance with Rabbi Yosei, let it teach here “and two heads came out as one”: even though they coincided exactly, since it is possible for births to coincide exactly, only one is consecrated, since the Merciful One restricted “the males.” And furthermore, we find a baraita that teaches: “and two heads came out as one, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says: Both go to the priest, as it is stated: ‘The males shall be the Lord’s.’”
gershom:a23.1: But when this “the males shall be the Lord’s” is written, it is written about inherent sanctity; how can he derive a firstborn donkey from it? Rather, because “the males shall be the Lord’s” is stated with a firstborn kosher animal, we derive a firstborn donkey from it as well. And if the mishna were Rabbi Yosei’s, let the mishna also teach “and they came out [as one].” Rather, since it does not teach it, learn from this that it is not Rabbi Yosei but the Rabbis, and this is a refutation of Abaye.
rashi:b1.1: Let us say the Rabbis hold that a portion of the womb: touching the firstborn, sanctifies it. For granted that it is impossible for the births to coincide exactly, and the first alone is sanctified, one can still object: before it came out entirely, its brother came out and interposed between it and the womb, and it is written: “Whatever opens any womb” (Numbers 8:16), [which means] it must open the entire womb. According to Rabbi Yosei there is no objection: since both are consecrated, they are like one.
rashi:b2.1: A substance with the same type of substance: and these two are of one type.
rashi:b5.1: And it is permitted: before its redemption.
rashi:b5.2: A firstborn son: it is permitted to benefit from his labor before his redemption, since we do not find that it is forbidden.
rashi:b5.3: About which the Torah was particular etc.: since [the Torah] is so stringent that the verse fixed its redemption with a lamb and not with anything else, it is certainly forbidden to derive benefit from it.
rashi:b6.2: At its value: he gives the priest greens worth the value of the donkey.
rashi:b6.3: We are not speaking of at its value: since it is no more stringent than consecrated property.
rashi:b6.4: To abrogate its forbidden status with a lamb: even not at its value, as the mishna teaches: “older or younger.”
rashi:b7.1: With a minted coin: since it is not desacralized onto an unminted coin [asimon], as it is written: “And bind up the money in your hand” (Deuteronomy 14:25).
rashi:b7.2: Intentionally: he meant to desacralize it.
rashi:b7.3: He has betrothed: if he betrothed a woman with it, she is betrothed. Evidently, according to Rabbi Yehuda, it is permitted to derive benefit from it.
rashi:b9.1: With that difference: since the donkey is worth more than the lamb.
rashi:b10.1: Whose redemption is permitted: as here, where the priest eats the lamb without any offering, while [the donkey] is forbidden before redemption? For with disqualified consecrated animals, which are forbidden for benefit before their redemption, their redemption takes on their sanctity and is forbidden.
rashi:b11.1: The Sabbatical Year: one who sells Sabbatical produce: the money is permitted forever, while the produce itself must be removed at the time of removal, when it is gone [from the field] for the wild animals. And the one who raised this objection thought that the redemption of Sabbatical produce is permitted forever, and had not heard that the very last item takes on its status.
rashi:b12.1: The very last: in tractate Sukkah (40b): if he purchased meat with Sabbatical produce, both must be removed at the time of removal. If he purchased wine with the meat, the meat goes out and the wine comes in; [oil with the wine,] the wine goes out and the oil comes in. And the last takes on Sabbatical status, to be removed. And the produce itself that grew in the Sabbatical Year, from which these came, is forbidden wherever it is, from the time of removal onward.
rashi:b13.1: Yours and that of others: gentiles; for example, a firstborn animal in which a gentile has a partnership. Although Rabbi Yehuda obligates [the owner] to give half its value to the priest, it is permitted for shearing and labor, since there is no sanctity in halves. But a firstborn donkey is not excluded by this verse, and so long as it is not excluded we do not permit it, since it is no less [stringent] than a firstborn kosher animal. According to Rabbi Shimon, the verse excludes it.
rashi:b18.1: Granted, according to Rabbi Yehuda: who expounds “your flock,” and not one in partnership with a gentile.
rashi:b18.2: That is why “your flock” is written: which implies that which is exclusively yours; it does not write “flock” without qualification. And “your ox”: even though it could have written “the firstborn of an ox,” and a firstborn son would also be excluded by it, even so it wrote “your ox” because of “your flock.”
rashi:b18.3: This is the reading: “That is why ‘your flock’ is written, and ‘your ox’ because of ‘your flock.’ But according to Rabbi Shimon, let it write ‘ox’ and ‘flock.’”
rashi:b19.1: We read: “Rava said.” [The printed text and the English read Rabba.]
rashi:b19.2: After the breaking of the neck: if he did not redeem it and broke its neck in accordance with its law.
rashi:b19.3: It is forbidden: [even] to feed it to his dog.
rashi:b21.1: A heifer whose neck is broken: is forbidden for benefit, because of [the verbal analogy of] “there” and “there”: there shall be its burial.
rashi:b21.2: And an ox that was to be stoned: that he slaughtered after its sentence was concluded, so that it did not come to the impurity of a carcass. And a heifer whose neck is broken: that he slaughtered after it had gone down to the stream with a strong current, since we hold that this renders it forbidden.
rashi:b21.3: The birds of a leper: are forbidden for benefit, in tractate Kiddushin (57a).
rashi:b21.4: And a firstborn donkey: that he slaughtered while it is still convulsing, so it has not come to the impurity of a carcass; but if a creeping animal touched it, it contracts the impurity of food, so that if it then touched other food it renders it impure, even though it is still convulsing. As it says in the chapter HaOr VehaRotev (Ḥullin 117b): one who slaughters a non-kosher animal for a gentile while it is convulsing, it contracts the impurity of food, since a Jew’s slaughter is effective as an intention [to make it food], since slaughter of that kind is fitting for a kosher animal. Alternatively, even if he actually broke its neck, so that it is a carcass, one can speak of food impurity for them, for example where there is less than an olive-bulk of them, which is not enough for the impurity of a carcass, and it combines with less than an egg-bulk of food to complete the egg-bulk.
rashi:b21.5: All of them are susceptible to the impurity of food: if impurity touched them. Even though they themselves are forbidden, [their status as food] is effective in this respect: if they touched other food, they render it impure.
rashi:b22.1: All of them are not susceptible: since they are forbidden for benefit.
rashi:b22.2: A period of susceptibility: before cooking.
rashi:b23.1: To others: to gentiles, since [such food] is not forbidden for benefit.
tosafot:b2.1: In brief: [Tosafot read “Rav Ashi said”; the printed Gemara and the English read Rav.] (1) Tosafot ask why, if a substance with its own kind does not interpose, the Gemara in Ḥullin 70a raises a dilemma about a fetus whose sister wrapped around it and brought it out. Three answers: here part of the womb is free, so it is more reasonable to say that its own kind does not interpose; or a sister is less “its own kind” than a brother; or the doubt there arises only because the sister helped bring it out, and had she not, it would plainly not interpose. (2) According to Abaye, who sets the mishna in line with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili (births can coincide) and still gives one lamb because of “the males,” why not apply the rule “whatever cannot take effect one after the other cannot take effect at once,” so that neither is consecrated? They answer that the rule applies only to what depends on an act, such as betrothing two sisters at once or a thanks offering slaughtered with eighty loaves, not to sanctity that comes of itself, even though one could ask which of the two is included. (3) The Gemara’s wording “granted that it is impossible to coincide, there is in any event interposition” seems to imply that if coinciding were possible there would be a difficulty without interposition, which the previous answer rules out. They explain the wording: granted that, since coinciding is impossible, the Rabbis cannot use “the males” as Rabbi Yosei does, there should nevertheless be interposition. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b3.1: In order to abrogate its forbidden status: since to exempt it from the mitzva of breaking the neck he would not need to designate a lamb out of uncertainty; just as he does not give [a lamb] to the priest out of uncertainty, so too he does not break its neck out of uncertainty.
tosafot:b7.1: And we learned: Rabbi Yehuda says: [If he did so] intentionally, he has betrothed: This implies that she is betrothed outside Jerusalem, before [the tithe] reaches Jerusalem. And what is said at the end of the chapter Ḥelek (Sanhedrin 112b), that outside Jerusalem all agree [dough of second tithe] is exempt from ḥalla, is not because it is considered property of the Most High outside Jerusalem according to all, but because “your dough” does not apply to it, since it is forbidden to eat [there]. Likewise, [property of second tithe in] an idolatrous city is not “its spoils,” as it says there. In the chapter HaSokher et HaPoalim (Bava Metzia 90a) too, Rabbi Yehuda exempts second tithe outside the wall from [the prohibition of] muzzling, not because it is considered property of the Most High outside the wall, but because we require the threshing to be fit for [the animal to eat], as we exclude consecrated property from misuse [me’ila].
tosafot:b23.1: “All food therein that may be eaten”: food that you can feed to others is called food: And if you say: in the chapter Kisui HaDam (Ḥullin 85a), according to Rabbi Shimon we exempt a non-kosher bird from covering [its blood], concerning a slaughter that does not render it fit, since it is written: “Any beast or bird that may be eaten”; but that is food you can feed to others! One may answer: there, “beast or bird” is written, which implies that it comes to exclude non-kosher species, which are not eaten by Jews, even though one can feed them to others. But here, “all food that may be eaten” properly implies excluding what may not be fed to others.
gershom:b1.1: And the Rabbis: of the mishna, who say he gives one lamb to the priest, since we established the mishna in accordance with the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yosei: let us say the Rabbis hold. [A parenthesis in the text: “And the Rabbis,” whether for the Rabbis or for Rabbi Yosei, it says “let us say.”] And some say: “And the Rabbis” who disagree with Rabbi Yosei in the other chapter, when two heads came out as one, who say “one is his and one is the priest’s”: let us say the Rabbis hold that touching part of the walls of the womb sanctifies, since when these come out together the womb touches each of them on one side only.
gershom:b2.1: As, if the entire womb sanctifies: that is, we require that it touch the firstborn on all sides. Granted that they disagree about whether it is impossible for births to coincide exactly, since the Rabbis hold that one pushes its head out farther than its fellow,
gershom:b3.1: There is in any event interposition: since each one interposes for its fellow, so that the womb did not touch all around it.
gershom:b4.1: Rav Ashi said [the printed Gemara and the English read Rav]: One cannot infer from here that we do not require the entire womb to sanctify. Even though here the womb did not touch each one all around, since both fetuses are of one kind, a substance with its own kind does not interpose, and it is considered as if the womb touched all around each one.
gershom:b5.1: Since it is the Israelite’s own, why do I need him to designate it?
gershom:b6.1: To abrogate from it the forbidden status of a firstborn donkey, so that the donkey will be permitted for shearing and labor.
gershom:b7.1: But there is a firstborn son, who requires redemption and from whose labor one may benefit even before he is redeemed.
gershom:b8.1: With shilkei: with boiled greens. He gave the priest some of the boiled greens at its value, however much the firstborn was worth, and redeemed it.
gershom:b9.1: We are not speaking of at its value: if he wants to redeem it at its value, the Torah was not particular about it [to say] that he can redeem it only with a lamb. And this is what it means: do you have an item about which the Torah was particular to abrogate its forbidden status with a lamb? That is, when he does not want to redeem it at its value, he can abrogate its forbidden status only with a lamb.
gershom:b10.1: But there is tithe, about which the Torah was particular that one cannot desacralize it onto an unminted coin, only onto minted silver; and we learned in tractate Kiddushin: “Rabbi Yehuda says: Intentionally, he has betrothed”: if he intentionally betrothed a woman with it, she is betrothed, and the reason is explained there. Evidently it is permitted for benefit. Rabbi Yehuda could say to you: you cannot challenge me from the betrothal of a woman, since with regard to betrothal she is betrothed with a firstborn donkey too, as Rabbi Elazar [says]: a woman knows etc. Here too, after the woman is betrothed with a firstborn donkey, she redeems it with a lamb and is betrothed to him with the difference between them, the surplus by which the firstborn donkey is worth more than the lamb, which is fully non-sacred. But [the donkey] itself, before it is redeemed, is forbidden for benefit, as I have said.
gershom:b11.1: Do you have an item whose redemption is permitted for benefit: since sanctity does not take hold of its redemption, for if he redeemed it with a lamb or with money, the priest can sell it or give it as a gift to whomever he wishes, and it is not forbidden for benefit to the one he gives it to; and the redeemed item is forbidden for benefit?
gershom:b12.1: And is there not? But there is the Sabbatical Year, whose redemption is permitted for benefit, since there is no sanctity in it, while [the produce] itself is forbidden. With the Sabbatical Year too, the redemption is forbidden, as the Master said: the very last takes on Sabbatical status, and the produce itself is forbidden; as it says: if he purchased meat with Sabbatical produce, and wine with the meat, etc.
gershom:b13.1: But you may work with yours and that of others: where a gentile has a partnership in it. “Your flock” was needed to exclude this case of partnership with a gentile, which is permitted for shearing and labor even before redemption. But your own firstborn, in which no one else has a partnership, even a firstborn donkey, is forbidden for benefit and for shearing and labor; this is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Shimon says: “You shall do no work with the firstborn of your ox,” but you may work with a firstborn son, whose labor is permitted; “nor shear the firstborn of your flock,” but you may shear a firstborn donkey, since Rabbi Shimon holds that a firstborn donkey is permitted in these.
gershom:b14.1: Granted, according to Rabbi Shimon: who establishes “You shall do no work with the firstborn of your ox” as permitting work with a firstborn son, and “the firstborn of your flock” as permitting the shearing of a firstborn donkey: that is why two verses are written.
gershom:b15.1: But according to Rabbi Yehuda, why do I need two verses? And furthermore, according to Rabbi Yehuda, who does not exclude work with a firstborn son, shall we say he too is forbidden for benefit?
gershom:b16.1: And where the verse was needed for Rabbi Yehuda is to permit [an animal in] partnership with a gentile for shearing and labor, after he has given half its value to the priest.
gershom:b17.1: And Rabbi Shimon holds that [an animal in] partnership with a gentile is entirely exempt, and no verse was needed to permit shearing and labor in a partnership. It was needed for shearing a firstborn donkey, and the same is true of labor, since it is permitted for benefit.
gershom:b18.1: Granted, according to Rabbi Yehuda: who establishes it as excluding [an animal in] partnership with a gentile, which is exempt [from the restrictions] on shearing and labor: that is why “your flock” is written, that is, yours and not yours and others’. And since it had to write “your flock” rather than “flock,” it also wrote “your ox” because it wrote “your flock”; “ox” would suffice to exclude a firstborn son, but it wrote “your ox” because of “your flock.”
gershom:b19.1: But according to Rabbi Shimon: who does not exclude a partnership, why do I need “your ox” and “your flock”? “The firstborn of an ox” and “the firstborn of a flock” would suffice. It is difficult.
gershom:b20.1: After the breaking of the neck: that he broke its neck with a cleaver; it is forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b21.1: From the heifer whose neck is broken: just as the heifer whose neck is broken is forbidden for benefit, since “there” and “there” is derived from “and [Miriam] died there,” it is forbidden for benefit like a corpse.
gershom:b22.1: And an ox that was to be stoned: that he slaughtered after its sentence was concluded; had it been stoned, it would impart the severe impurity of a carcass with an olive-bulk.
gershom:b23.1: And a heifer whose neck is broken: that he slaughtered after it went down to the stream with a strong current.
gershom:b24.1: And a firstborn donkey: as we say, one who slaughters a non-kosher animal for a gentile while it is still convulsing: it is susceptible to the impurity of food, since the intention of slaughter prepares it to contract the impurity of food; and when it dies, it imparts severe impurity with an olive-bulk, like the carcass of a non-kosher animal that died.
gershom:b25.1: All of them are susceptible to the impurity of food: as we said, even though they are forbidden for benefit.
gershom:b26.1: Rabbi Shimon says: All of them are not susceptible to the impurity of food, since they are forbidden for benefit and had no period of fitness: for orla [the text corrects “for the heifer” to “for orla”]; and for the ox, the heifer and the birds, we say that an animal in its lifetime stands in a presumption of prohibition until you know with what it was slaughtered. Except for meat in milk: even though it is forbidden for benefit, it is susceptible to the impurity of food, since it had a period of fitness before it was mixed and cooked.
gershom:b27.1: And Rabbi Asi says: What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon, who says all of them are not susceptible to the impurity of food? Since they are food that you cannot feed to others, even to gentiles, because they are forbidden for benefit, they are not called food.
